description: Designs feature-flag systems and lifecycle policy - flag taxonomy (release, ops/kill-switch, experiment, permission), percentage rollouts with stable bucketing, safe defaults, and mandatory removal deadlines so flags don't rot into dead code. Use when someone asks "how should I roll this out behind a flag", "kill switch vs feature flag", "how do I do a percentage rollout", "we have hundreds of stale flags", or is wiring up LaunchDarkly or a homegrown flag service. Do NOT use for designing the A/B test analysis itself - use ab-test-analyzer instead - and do NOT use for CI/CD pipeline gating - use github-actions instead.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not create a flag without an owner and removal deadline - flag debt is the default outcome, not the exception.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not create a flag without an owner and removal deadline - flag debt is the default outcome, not the exception.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not reuse a release flag as a permanent kill switch; recreate it deliberately as an ops flag with its own testing schedule.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not reuse a release flag as a permanent kill switch; recreate it deliberately as an ops flag with its own testing schedule.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not change experiment allocation mid-experiment or use non-sticky assignment - both invalidate the results.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not change experiment allocation mid-experiment or use non-sticky assignment - both invalidate the results.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not nest flags into combinations (`flagA && !flagB`); the test matrix goes exponential and untested interactions ship.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not nest flags into combinations (`flagA && !flagB`); the test matrix goes exponential and untested interactions ship.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not bucket on session id or random-per-request - users flip between variants and support tickets become unreproducible.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not bucket on session id or random-per-request - users flip between variants and support tickets become unreproducible.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not let the flag service become a hard dependency; an outage at the provider must degrade to safe defaults, not errors.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not let the flag service become a hard dependency; an outage at the provider must degrade to safe defaults, not errors.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Do not use different bucketing keys across services - a user must see one variant everywhere.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Do not use different bucketing keys across services - a user must see one variant everywhere.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: For designing the experiment metrics and reading significance, use ab-test-analyzer. For gating deploys rather than features, use github-actions or vercel-deploy-pipeline. If a flag flip is the response to an active incident, pair with sev-triage.

workflow_steps.evidence: Flags decouple deploy from release: code ships dark and turns on safely, in stages, with an instant off switch. The costly mistake this skill prevents is flag debt - every flag is a fork in your codebase that doubles the test matrix, and a flag without an owner and a removal deadline set at creation becomes permanent dead code that someone flips three years later during an incident with no idea what it does.
workflow_steps.text: Flags decouple deploy from release: code ships dark and turns on safely, in stages, with an instant off switch. The costly mistake this skill prevents is flag debt - every flag is a fork in your codebase that doubles the test matrix, and a flag without an owner and a removal deadline set at creation becomes permanent dead code that someone flips three years later during an incident with no idea what it does.

workflow_steps.evidence: - Release flag: gates unfinished or risky features during rollout. Lifetime: days to weeks. Removal deadline set at creation, maximum 90 days out; most should die within 30 days of full rollout.
workflow_steps.text: - Release flag: gates unfinished or risky features during rollout. Lifetime: days to weeks. Removal deadline set at creation, maximum 90 days out; most should die within 30 days of full rollout.

workflow_steps.evidence: - Ops flag / kill switch: disables a feature or dependency during an incident. Long-lived by design, but the inventory must stay small (a service with 50 kill switches has 50 untested code paths) and each must be re-tested on a schedule - flip it in staging at least quarterly, because an untested kill switch fails exactly when you need it.
workflow_steps.text: - Ops flag / kill switch: disables a feature or dependency during an incident. Long-lived by design, but the inventory must stay small (a service with 50 kill switches has 50 untested code paths) and each must be re-tested on a schedule - flip it in staging at least quarterly, because an untested kill switch fails exactly when you need it.

workflow_steps.evidence: - Experiment flag: A/B test with metrics. Lifetime equals the experiment duration plus one decision week. When the experiment concludes, the losing branch and the flag are deleted in the same PR that records the result.
workflow_steps.text: - Experiment flag: A/B test with metrics. Lifetime equals the experiment duration plus one decision week. When the experiment concludes, the losing branch and the flag are deleted in the same PR that records the result.

workflow_steps.evidence: - Permission flag: gates by plan or entitlement. This is not a temporary flag - it is product configuration. Model it as entitlements data, not in the same system as release flags, or it will pollute every "stale flag" report forever.

Pass its `workspace_id` explicitly on every `well_*` call below, and never merge data across workspaces in one run. workflow_steps.evidence:
Two-sided beats one-sided: reward the referrer and discount the friend. A
one-sided reward makes the recommendation feel like a commission ("is he
recommending them for the fifty bucks?"); two-sided lets the referrer open
with a gift ("use these guys, you'll get $50 off"), which preserves the
social framing that makes referrals work. Summit's design: $50 service
credit to the referrer, $50 off the friend's first job. Against a $450
average ticket at 55 percent margin, a $100 total incentive still lands the
customer far below the $119 paid CAC - and the referred customer closes
better and refers onward. Size the incentive at roughly 10-25 percent of
average ticket total across both sides. Keep redemption dead simple: "have
them mention your name," tracked in a spreadsheet - no codes, no portal.

workflow_steps.evidence: **Diagnosing flaky tests**: Isolate the test with `--test-only` → check for shared state or timer dependencies → inspect async teardown order → add retry logic as a temporary diagnostic step → fix root cause. See [rules/flaky-tests.md](rules/flaky-tests.md).

constraints_boundaries.evidence:
When the cursor falls outside the bounded replay window or is ahead of the current
host stream, the server emits `stream.gap`. Its payload includes `reason`,
`requestedAfterSequence`, `firstAvailableSequence`, `lastAvailableSequence`, and
`resumeAfterSequence`. The connection continues from `resumeAfterSequence` and sends
any retained matching notifications, but the client must first reload canonical run
detail/events because the missing notifications cannot be reconstructed from SSE.

constraints_boundaries.evidence:
The stream is pinned to the active database profile and runtime generation. A profile
switch cancels existing subscriptions. Reconnect against the new profile and rebuild
state from durable APIs; do not reuse an SSE cursor across a profile switch or process
restart.

workflow_steps.evidence: Almost every freelance dispute - unpaid invoices, endless revisions, "that was obviously included" - traces back to a scope document that only listed what IS included and stayed silent on everything else. A dispute-preventing SOW is defined as much by its exclusions as its inclusions, and it decides in advance how three predictable events get handled: the client asks for more, the client goes quiet, and the client won't say "done". This skill writes that document.

description: Writes "read next," "related articles," or "previously on" teaser blocks for web pages, newsletters, or app interfaces — short, click-worthy summaries that drive readers from one piece of content to another.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - Teaser quality depends heavily on the source material provided. If the user supplies only a vague headline and no description, the teaser will necessarily be generic. Providing a two-sentence summary of each article's angle produces significantly better teasers.
constraints_boundaries.text: - Teaser quality depends heavily on the source material provided. If the user supplies only a vague headline and no description, the teaser will necessarily be generic. Providing a two-sentence summary of each article's angle produces significantly better teasers.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - The assistant optimizes teasers for editorial click-through but cannot predict actual performance. Headline A/B testing and analytics should inform teaser strategy over time.
constraints_boundaries.text: - The assistant optimizes teasers for editorial click-through but cannot predict actual performance. Headline A/B testing and analytics should inform teaser strategy over time.

constraints_boundaries.evidence: - This skill writes text teasers only. It does not generate thumbnail images, select featured images, or produce visual teaser cards. For visual elements, pair with an image prompting skill or provide image selections separately.
constraints_boundaries.text: - This skill writes text teasers only. It does not generate thumbnail images, select featured images, or produce visual teaser cards. For visual elements, pair with an image prompting skill or provide image selections separately.

workflow_steps.evidence: 1. **Identifies the hook in each article.** Reads the provided material and finds the single most compelling element — the fact, question, or revelation that would make a reader click. This becomes the core of the teaser, not a generic summary.
workflow_steps.text: 1. **Identifies the hook in each article.** Reads the provided material and finds the single most compelling element — the fact, question, or revelation that would make a reader click. This becomes the core of the teaser, not a generic summary.

workflow_steps.evidence: 2. **Writes each teaser as a self-contained unit.** Every teaser must work on its own — a reader encountering it in a sidebar or newsletter should understand what the article offers without needing additional context. The teaser answers: "What will I learn or experience if I click this?"
workflow_steps.text: 2. **Writes each teaser as a self-contained unit.** Every teaser must work on its own — a reader encountering it in a sidebar or newsletter should understand what the article offers without needing additional context. The teaser answers: "What will I learn or experience if I click this?"

workflow_steps.evidence: 3. **Differentiates teasers from each other.** When writing a block of 3–5 teasers, ensures each one uses a different hook structure (question, statistic, bold claim, scene-setting detail) so the block does not feel repetitive. Variety in opening structure increases the chance that at least one teaser resonates with any given reader.
workflow_steps.text: 3. **Differentiates teasers from each other.** When writing a block of 3–5 teasers, ensures each one uses a different hook structure (question, statistic, bold claim, scene-setting detail) so the block does not feel repetitive. Variety in opening structure increases the chance that at least one teaser resonates with any given reader.

workflow_steps.evidence: 4. **Matches the teaser style to the placement context.** Sidebar teasers are tighter and more utilitarian. Newsletter teasers can be warmer and more conversational. Homepage teasers lean toward urgency and newsworthiness. End-of-article "read next" teasers connect thematically to what the reader just finished.

workflow_steps.evidence: 5. **Formats for the specified layout.** Each teaser includes the elements requested: headline (or reformulated teaser headline), summary sentence(s), and optional metadata (category, date, reading time). Output is structured so a web editor or newsletter builder can drop teasers directly into the layout.
